items.title: NYC, LA and Chicago School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
items.summary: Google’s refusal to unbundle A.I. features from search for students prompted a backlash. Now schools are looking for alternatives.
items.full_text:
Title: NYC, LA and Chicago School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/google-gemini-ai-search-schools-nyc-la-chicago.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:28:57 GMT

Markdown Content:
Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.

Starting next year, Google [said](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html), its products for schools will no longer have A.I. turned on automatically. Rather, administrators will now have to choose to turn A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A.I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A.I. will lose access to an important learning tool.

Google’s approach created a firestorm of [criticism from lawmakers](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/business/google-ai-school-features.html), government officials, education leaders and parents, some of whom said the tech giant was trying to [force its A.I. into public schools](https://x.com/NYCMayor/status/2117692668213940677).

Now, some schools across the United States are blocking Google’s A.I. in search — or considering alternative providers.

“If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”

Google’s new use-it-or-lose-it stance on A.I. in search underscores how the tech giant’s interlocking ecosystem of Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs has become essential classroom infrastructure. The company’s search engine is a go-to product for teaching students how to do research and find primary sources.

But some educators worry that the generative A.I. that Google has embedded in its search engine for consumers could hinder students’ critical thinking, undermine learning and present safety risks. Some students have used the chatbots embedded in search to cheat, they have said, or scanned A.I.-generated search summaries instead of reading historical documents and news sources.

Educators are balancing those concerns with the reality that A.I. has already become an important tool in the work force, that a majority of U.S. teenagers already use chatbots and that many students will need to use A.I. in their future jobs.

Medical associations have also warned that developing relationships with chatbots could have negative mental health effects on young people. Earlier this month, two parents in North Carolina [sued Google](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/technology/ai-safety-school-chromebooks-google-lawsuit.html), saying their daughter had developed a plan to die by suicide after prolonged chats with the company’s A.I. on search on her school Chromebook. (Google said it had built safeguards into its A.I. features in search to help young people find emergency resources and was reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.)

Now districts like Chicago Public Schools, the fourth-largest U.S. school system, are urging Google to provide them with a version of search without A.I. features. “If such an arrangement can’t be reached,” Chicago Public Schools said in an email, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

Among the search engine alternatives for schools: DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing. Both [offer options](https://noai.duckduckgo.com/) to [disable A.I.-generated answers](https://blogs.bing.com/search/2026/11/your-choice-turn-ai-answers-on-or-off-in-bing/).

Google argued this month that it would be providing schools with more options to control student A.I. access — not fewer. Administrators could give students access to A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like function in search, as well as A.I. Overview, which summarizes search results, the company said. It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.

Image

Google’s new stance on A.I. in search underscores how Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs have become essential classroom infrastructure.Credit...David Robert Elliott for The New York Times

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”

Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A.I. a top business priority. And Google has [integrated its Gemini A.I.](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/10/technology/google-ai-products.html?) chatbot throughout its software suite.

The fight over Google’s A.I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A.I.

School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A.I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A.I. use.

“We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A.I. adoption is going to be.”

In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District [announced](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/nyregion/ai-ban-schools-nyc.html)[moratoriums](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/03/us/lausd-schools-ban-ai-artificial-intelligence.html) on student use of generative A.I.

At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A.I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A.I. features were so “[deeply integrated](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html)” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.

Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.

In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”

Video

[Video 3](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/11/17/183779_1_17visualUploader-46779_wg_mobile_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/17visualUploader-46779-cover/17visualUploader-46779-cover-videoSixteenByNine768.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)

Google said it was giving schools more A.I. options, even as the company declined to provide schools with a chatbot-free version of search.

“We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.

Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”

Image

Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.Credit...Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times

At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.

This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A.I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.

New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A.I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A.I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.

New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A.I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.

In the absence of A.I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to [block student access](https://www.lightspeedsystems.com/blog/block-google-ai-overview-ai-mode-students/) to A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode in Google search.

The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.

“Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A.I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

Matthew Haag contributed reporting.

items.title: Mark Carney Says Canada Will Not Back Down in Trade Talks With U.S.
items.summary: Conversely, the prime minister of Canada said that talks with China were “going exceptionally well.”
items.full_text:
Title: Mark Carney Says Canada Will Not Back Down in Trade Talks With U.S. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/business/dealbook/mark-carney-canada-us-trade.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:25:31 GMT

Markdown Content:
Canada’s relationship with the Trump administration continues to look frosty. But its efforts to bolster ties with China are showing promise.

Appearing remotely from Shenzhen, China, after long day of meetings, including a session with President Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Canada would not back down in its trade battle with the United States.

On the other hand, he said talks with China were “going exceptionally well.”

“We reached an agreement, we reduced tariffs in over 90 percent of trade irritants,” he said. “And of course, I’m speaking about our trade negotiations with China. They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”

He added: “Now, if you’re asking about the United States, well, we continue to have a series of issues there.”

Mr. Carney is wrapping up an eight-day tour, which has taken him from Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia and finally China for the APEC summit. All of it in the cause of diversifying Canada’s economy away from its heavy dependence on the United States.

Asked if he now trusts Xi Jinping, China’s leader, more than Mr. Trump, Mr. Carney offered an indirect reply. “We look for situations where there is alignment, and we trust alignment,” he said.

Mr. Carney emphasized, as he has in the past, that Canada’s expanded relationship with China would have careful guardrails. And he dismissed the idea that Canada’s growing relationship with China would leave Canada trading one dependence for another, saying, for example, that he did not think selling canola, an oil seed, to China would be “compromising our sovereignty.”

Before a leaders’ dinner Wednesday evening in China, Mr. Carney had an unscheduled meeting with Mr. Trump. It did not advance Canada’s cause in the trade talks, the prime minister said.

“We had a very nice discussion this evening, so I’ll hang on to that,” Mr. Carney said. “Look, has it changed? I would say no is the short answer.”

Any resolution of the trade war, which had place tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian auto, steel and aluminum exports, will take a major change in policy in Washington, Mr. Carney said. The prime minister also rejected Mr. Trump’s repeated assertions that Canada had no leverage in negotiations with Washington.

“Our cards is that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said.

items.title: Nepal Came to COP31 in Dire Need. It’s a Test for the World.
items.summary: A deadly glacier collapse left the country with $5 billion in recovery costs. So far, few have stepped up with aid.
items.full_text:
Title: Nepal Came to COP31 in Dire Need. It’s a Test for the World. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/climate/nepal-disaster-aid-cop31.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:18:43 GMT

Markdown Content:
After the devastating glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500, Nepal arrived at the U.N. climate talks in Turkey looking for help.

What it found was a system that many say is ill-equipped to help vulnerable countries recover from climate disasters.

The catastrophe in August occurred after a wall of rock and ice crumbled, setting off a flood that [wiped away towns and left thousands missing](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/world/asia/nepal-tibet-floods-school-children.html). Nepal says it will cost roughly $5 billion to rebuild.

But so far, Nepal has received pledges for less than 10 percent of that amount, with much of it in the form of loans.

The devastation in Nepal has become a crucial test case for whether the global community can deliver quick financial relief when disasters strike. Many at the talks, including Nepal and small island nations whose low-lying countries face repeated typhoons and storm damage, said getting help to rebuild could take months or even years, a delay they can’t afford.

“Our melting mountains cannot wait for our negotiations to catch up with their changing reality,” Shisir Khanal, the Nepali foreign minister, told leaders at the climate summit, known as COP31.

This week, an effort by Nepal and Bhutan to make glacial ice melt and other issues facing mountain communities a formal part of the climate negotiations stalled. At the same time, a fund created to help vulnerable countries cope with the economic consequences of climate disasters has promised Nepal just $21.6 million, a tiny fraction of its need.

“We are suffering from a disaster which we did not cause,” said Pramesh Pokharel, a Nepali activist who works with small-scale farmers. “Most greenhouse gas emissions are caused by the global north, rich people and multinational corporations.”

Developed nations and rich companies should foot the bill for Nepal’s recovery, Mr. Pokharel said.

“It’s about who bears the cost of the loss and damages, and who should pay,” he said. “We are demanding that those who are polluting, they must pay the cost of the devastation we are facing.”

Image

A “Climate Justice for Nepal” demonstration at the COP31 venue in Antalya, Turkey, on Tuesday.Credit...Murad Sezer/Reuters

In the months since the disaster, Nepal has received patchwork pledges from around the globe. The World Bank said it would make $170 million in emergency financing available.

The United States initially offered $500,000 in aid, then expanded that sum to $36 million after Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia, pledged $10 million.

A handful of countries, including Australia and Japan, pledged a combined $40 million. The United Nations helped raise an additional $50 million.

The four entities that have historically provided Nepal with the most support are India, China, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

All those pledges still fall short. Assessments conducted in the days after the catastrophe concluded that damages totaled about $1.8 billion. Rebuilding the devastated areas with improved infrastructure, the government concluded, would cost roughly $5 billion, equivalent to about 10 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product.

After the Aug. 26 glacier collapse, the Loss and Damage Fund, which was [created in 2024 under the U.N. climate treaty framework](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/17/climate/loss-damage-fund-cop29-baku.html) to help nations recover from climate-fueled disasters, held a special meeting to allow Nepal to submit a fast-track proposal for aid, which led to the $21.6 million commitment.

“When Nepal happened, there was a lot of pressure from all of us,” said Ibrahima Cheikh Diong, executive director of the Loss and Damage Fund. “This is why the fund was set up. Even though we’re not sitting on billions of dollars, our board couldn’t afford to just do nothing.”

Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, said his country’s need remained enormous.

“When the need is $5 billion, $20 million is nothing,” Mr. Waglé said. “However, this is acknowledging that very poor countries, the low-income countries in the fragile Himalayas, are bearing the brunt of the Western industrialization.”

This week the Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, is in India seeking a $2 billion package of credits, loans and grants. Nepal was also looking to China to help it rebuild its physical infrastructure destroyed by the flood, which included the main trading corridor between the two countries, Mr. Waglé said. And it was seeking below-market-rate loans as well as grants from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, he said.

“I request the U.S. to step up,” Mr. Waglé said. “We’re in this together and cooperation demands that we have to help countries in need.”

Nepal has called the glacier collapse a climate disaster. World Weather Attribution, a scientific group, said that the conditions that led to the collapse had been made [more likely because of human-caused climate change.](https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/rapid-warming-in-the-himalaya-exacerbates-geohazard-cascades-beyond-adaptation-limits/)

“The permafrost thawing and the glaciers melting, that’s a direct cause of global warming,” Mr. Waglé said. “Because of global warming, ice is retreating, glaciers are melting, and this rock got exposed to the elements, and that accentuated the vulnerability.”

The disaster in Nepal has forced leaders from other developing nations to find new ways of seeking assistance. This week President Keiko Fujimori of Peru appealed directly to President Xi Jinping of China for aid to help cope with the effects of El Niño. She walked away with a pledge of $22.5 million.

Pacific island nations have started a type of endowment fund to help disaster-proof their countries and “cut out the red tape,” President Surangel Whipps Jr. of Palau said.

items.title: OpenAI Executives Say They Have to Strike a Balance Between A.I. Safety and Progress
items.summary: The company’s C.E.O., Sam Altman, and president, Greg Brockman, said they cannot “make everybody happy.”
items.full_text:
Title: OpenAI Executives Say They Have to Strike a Balance Between A.I. Safety and Progress - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/business/dealbook/openai-sam-altman-greg-brockman.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:25:49 GMT

Markdown Content:
OpenAI’s chief executive said Wednesday that pushing the safe advancement of artificial intelligence comes with inherent trade-offs, and the company had to strike a balance between prioritizing safety while continuing progress on developing A.I.

“We’re not going to be able to make everybody happy,” Sam Altman said at the DealBook Summit

If OpenAI only focuses on being “max pedal to the metal,” he added, “People will say, ‘Well, you know, please don’t kill us all.’”

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has been under heightened scrutiny in recent months after its A.I. agents went rogue and hacked companies, including the [open-source A.I. platform Hugging Face](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/), and [government systems](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/technology/openais-ai-us-government-websites.html).

Those were learning experiences, Mr. Altman said. OpenAI follows “iterative deployment,” he added, and the “only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality,” suggesting that the risks couldn’t be known without having been tested in the real world.

OpenAI, along with other A.I. companies, has signed a voluntary agreement to conduct risk reviews and work with third-party evaluators. The company [said on Monday](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-top-5) that it was embedding independent safety researchers from third-party groups, including METR and Apollo Research, to evaluate OpenAI’s models against various safety measures.

“The models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new. And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift,” said Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder. “It’s not any one company. It’s really a whole industrywide shift.”

With its rival Anthropic on the verge of a public offering, Altman said OpenAI was still advancing toward its own I.P.O. “We plan to be a public company at some point,” Mr. Altman said.

Mr. Brockman has an equity stake worth at least $30 billion in OpenAI, but Mr. Altman famously owns no shares in the giant start-up. “When we were first setting up the structure, I said to him, ‘You should take equity,’” Mr. Brockman said, referring to the C.E.O.

“I should have listened to Greg,” Mr. Altman said, eliciting laughter. But he said that not having equity had not affected his work at OpenAI. “I don’t think you could argue that I have not acted with full commitment to the company.”

Mr. Brockman drew a contrast between his company’s structure and that of Anthropic, where the seven co-founders hold 50.1 percent of total voting control. “We’re the only company where the founders don’t have super majority control,” he said.

Mr. Altman has previously said the company is delaying its I.P.O. plans till next year to focus on safety issues. Earlier this month, OpenAI raised $11 billion as part of a fund-raising round [valued at $1.25 trillion.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/business/dealbook/tech-investors-ai-rout.html) That’s lower than the $30 billion it initially sought to raise at a valuation as [high as $1.5 trillion.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/business/dealbook/openai-new-funding-round.html)

Anthropic is expected to list its shares publicly on Thursday in what could be the world’s largest I.P.O. Earlier this month, Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, which would value the company at $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion.

items.title: Google Buys Worker Data From Spirit Airlines in a New Market to Feed A.I.
items.summary: A flight attendants’ union challenged Google’s plans to protect personal information in the data in court, saying the company’s measures were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.
items.full_text:
Title: Google Buys Worker Data From Spirit Airlines in a New Market to Feed A.I. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/business/economy/google-spirit-employee-data-ai.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:13:20 GMT

Markdown Content:
When Spirit Airlines [shut down in May](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/02/business/spirit-airlines-shutdown.html), its assets went up for sale: a small fleet of airplanes, [coveted slots](https://aviationweek.com/air-transport/airports-networks/jetblues-purchase-spirits-laguardia-slots-gets-faa-approval) at LaGuardia Airport and decades of internal workplace data, including employee records, tax forms, 100 million emails and half a billion Microsoft Teams messages.

Google had the winning bid, $10 million, for those employment records, a novel asset class the company said it would use to improve its artificial intelligence products. Imagine what a large language model could glean from the recruiting and timekeeping files of such a large company, or from workers’ snarky chats about their bosses.

But in August, a union representing 5,500 flight attendants affected by the bankruptcy filed an objection in federal court, saying that de-identifying measures promised by Google and Spirit, largely related to the protection of consumer data, were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.

“If it was not for our union, this would have just happened in a fire sale in the middle of the night,” said Sara Nelson, the president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “This is a brand-new frontier for workers’ rights. It’s making people’s lives, their entire privacy, a commodity.”

Last week, Google agreed to new limitations on the employee data. In a hearing on Tuesday, a bankruptcy judge in federal court in New York State accepted the revised sale terms, and the flight attendants’ union dropped its objections. A spokesman for Google said the company was happy with the result but declined to comment further until the court posted the full language of the agreement.

Image

Sara Nelson, the president of the flight attendants’ union, said: “This is a brand-new frontier for workers’ rights. It’s making people’s lives, their entire privacy, a commodity.”Credit...Heather Khalifa for The New York Times

Spirit said it was pleased that the court had approved the sale of data that would go through a “court-supervised exclusion and de-identification process” before its transfer to Google.

“This approval follows months of productive dialogue between Spirit, Google, the consumer privacy ombudsman, our labor unions and the other key stakeholders who have engaged constructively to ensure the sale is conducted in line with data privacy regulations and best practices,” a Spirit spokesman said.

Data has been sold before in bankruptcies that have raised consumer privacy concerns, like the 2025 [bankruptcy of 23andMe](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/10/business/23andme-data-lawsuit.html), a genetic testing service. And there are examples of a failed company’s records becoming public. After Enron, an energy company, collapsed in 2001, federal investigators released a trove of company emails. They have been mined for case studies and research.

But only recently have companies sought access to a failed company’s internal work force data. There is a market developing, largely out of sight, for the carcasses of dead companies to be turned into feasts for large language models with insatiable appetites for written communication. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has considered buying data from struggling start-ups, Bloomberg [reported in September](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-17/spacex-discusses-buying-data-for-ai-models-from-failed-startups).

The Spirit case appears to be the first large-scale example of using “corporate detritus” to train large language models, said Greg Ewing, a partner at Spencer Fane, a law firm. The idea is to teach A.I. how humans speak in the workplace.

“This is a whole new world, where all that data is so valuable to A.I. companies,” Mr. Ewing said. “We are going to see whole marketplaces arise out of it.”

Eric Chafetz, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler, a law firm, said the Spirit case was the first large bankruptcy sale in which a buyer had said it was motivated to build A.I. models. “We have recently received numerous unsolicited inbound inquiries from entities purporting to want to buy similar types of data,” he said. “Parties do believe there’s real value in trying to purchase a failed or failing company’s data.”

This has consequences for employees, Mr. Chafetz said: The bankruptcy code’s privacy protections were designed for consumers.“Employees aren’t in that picture at all,” he said.

Ms. Nelson said personnel files, even if they were cleared of identifying information, could be used to connect private data to a specific employee. A woman’s leave for reproductive care could one day be traced back to her. A pilot’s detailed background check, later uncovered, could expose sensitive personal details.

The flight attendants’ union, which is part of the AFL-CIO, wants to enshrine worker privacy protections into contracts and the law, she said.

“These are standards that can be put into law right away because we already have a major company working on the advancement of these A.I. models, who can comply with these very high standards of protections for workers,” Ms. Nelson said.

The union was joined in its efforts by other unions affected by the Spirit bankruptcy; in all, Ms. Nelson said, about 17,000 workers had been affected by the data privacy issue. In October, more than 120 congressional leaders [sent a letter](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/press/dem/release/cantwell-colleagues-urge-spirit-airlines-and-google-to-protect-workers-privacy-amid-sale-of-data-for-ai-training/) to Google and Spirit asking them to include more protections for employees.

The revised agreement makes clear that certain [information](https://afacwa.org/spirit-data-protections/) is not to be part of the sale, including employee medical and disability records, flight crew fatigue reports and payroll records.

Last week, lawyers for GE Aerospace and CFM International, parts suppliers to Spirit, asked the bankruptcy court to exclude data related to their companies, too, including information related to engine maintenance and avionics systems.

“The data sale poses significant risks to parties that provided such information to the debtors over the years, because Google may use or disclose it through its A.I. products,” they wrote.

items.title: A Massachusetts Town Revolts Against Amazon’s Delivery Drones
items.summary: Amazon wants to offer faster delivery. Residents want quiet skies. A Massachusetts suburb wages an epic battle for control of its airspace.
items.full_text:
Title: A Massachusetts Town Revolts Against Amazon’s Delivery Drones - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/amazon-delivery-drones-massachusetts.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:30:25 GMT

Markdown Content:
In a font that begged for a magnifying glass, right below the newspaper’s classified ads, there it was: Notice of Public Hearing.

Christine Farmer, a longtime resident of Westborough, Mass., normally skipped over legal notices in the weekly Community Advocate. But this time, she caught it by chance — a public hearing in mid-September on Amazon’s request to build a drone hub for its new delivery service. The project, which involved a staging area and launch zones, would be based at the company’s warehouse less than two miles from Ms. Farmer’s home.

It was the first time Ms. Farmer, a 63-year-old executive coach and business consultant, had heard about plans for drone deliveries in the region.

Like many of her neighbors in Westborough, Ms. Farmer loved Amazon. A few months earlier, she had nearly hugged an Amazon driver to thank him for bringing her a package — by electric van — that she needed that same day.

But the drone deliveries felt startling and unnecessary, she thought — an existential change.

Image

Christine Farmer asked, do we really need packages delivered by drones?

Were delivery drones really something Westborough needed, zipping over its ponds and parks, hiking trails and tall, tall trees?

Ms. Farmer’s decision to attend the meeting eventually led her to a place she never expected to be: in the thick of a growing rebellion against Amazon and its plans for drone delivery dominance across America.

In 2013, Amazon introduced the concept of widespread drone delivery as if it was a fait accompli, with its founder, Jeff Bezos, saying that it “will work, and it will happen.” The reason for it was simple, the company has said: customers demand ever faster service.

Amazon now has 20 drone hubs, and in August, and the company said that it aimed to expand drone deliveries to nearly 500 U.S. towns and cities, including more than 60 hubs, by the end of the year. Some local governments have readily approved the company’s plans.

“As residents learn more about it and see it for themselves, Prime Air is a welcome addition to communities,” said Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokeswoman, adding that the drone program reduces traffic on the road and brings highly skilled jobs.

Image

In August, Amazon announced that its drone service would expand to reach more than 500 towns and cities by the end of the year.Credit...Sophie Park for The New York Times

But some residents, like Ms. Farmer, are dreading an influx of 83-pound flying machines that seem straight out of “The Jetsons.” Zooming across the sky at up to 74 miles an hour, they look to some residents like colossal interplanetary insects and sound like a supersized swarm of locusts.

Opponents of the drones are fuming at the Federal Aviation Administration for ruling that commercial delivery drones would not significantly affect “the human environment” and that each location did not need a full environmental review. (The F.A.A. declined to comment.) And they are furious with local authorities for not doing more to push back against the impending changes to the sights and sounds of everyday life.

If Amazon drones come, Ms. Farmer asked, what would stop Walmart drones from following? Or DoorDash? Target? Home Depot?

“We will be living under a drone highway, and who would want that?” said Ms. Farmer, who raised two daughters in Westborough, a town of about 23,000 people, 30 miles west of Boston.

She continued, “I really just can’t imagine living in a world where the skies just aren’t quiet anymore.”

Image

Westborough, Mass., has 23,000 residents and an Amazon warehouse.

## The Battle Begins

Before the Westborough planning board meeting in mid-September, Ms. Farmer went out of her way to say a prayer at her church. She asked for guidance because she considered the drone issue to be “a tipping point for our country.”

At the [board meeting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lE8UzPj-Nns), she found only a handful of other residents, mostly there for other, more quotidian issues. They seemed surprised, Ms. Farmer thought, when Tareq Wafaie, an economic development manager for Amazon, delivered a presentation about Amazon’s Prime Air program. It would be the first drone delivery service in New England.

Mr. Wafaie explained that the drones are about five feet wide and five feet tall, have six arms with propellers, and can carry a single package that is five pounds or less. Customers opting in can get deliveries in 30 minutes or less, he said, with the drones dropping packages onto people’s yards or driveways from 13 feet up, without humans guiding them in real time.

The F.A.A., which governs the nation’s airspace, had cleared Amazon’s drone hub for up to 1,000 flights per day, from “about sunrise to sunset,” Mr. Wafaie said, and the drones can fly as far as 7.5 miles before circling back to their home base.

Ms. Farmer grabbed her phone and started calculating: If there were, say, 600 drone deliveries in 12 hours, that would mean almost one delivery every minute.

Several residents seemed to be thinking along similar lines. “The risk does not match the want,” Jen Parent, a teacher, told the board. “We’re at this point in our human history with technology, just because we can do it, doesn’t mean we should do it.”

One man said he couldn’t imagine the drones being quiet. Another said that drones were “cool,” but worried about privacy because their cameras could peer into yards.

A nervous Ms. Farmer fumbled with the microphone before taking it off its stand.

In a voice gentle enough to read bedtime stories, she explained that she had grown up in Winthrop, a town near Boston’s Logan Airport. Every day, all day long, she heard planes overhead.

“I just want to advise and really just say, you open the door to this and more will come,” she said to the planning board. “I implore that you continue to consider the sounds and the visuals. I love to walk. We love the nature.”

She added, “That’s why I moved here.”

The planning board postponed its decision. When Ms. Farmer got home, she told her husband, “Honey, this is not our wheelhouse. But we can’t stay silent.”

Image

Westborough residents formed Mass Blue Skies, a grassroots anti-drone group.

## A Growing Revolt

Steeped in the issue for what she called “a whole 30 seconds,” Ms. Farmer began posting about the drones on social media, to tell her neighbors.

At a [Sept. 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUtBSoJRk7g) meeting of the select board, the town’s policymaking body, the public was allowed to speak about the issue and Ms. Farmer got up — twice — to oppose Amazon’s plan.

Once Amazon begins its service, “there’s no turning back,” she warned, citing communities in Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska and [Texas, where residents say they feel trapped](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/21/us/politics/amazon-drone-delivery-texas.html) after their cities approved Amazon’s plans.

The next day, Amazon held an informational session at a local hotel. Ms. Farmer sat in a corner to listen to other residents speak, amazed that a coalition against the drones had grown so quickly.

More than 200 people squeezed into the room, including residents from nearby towns that would be affected.

For nearly three hours, Mr. Wafaie, of Amazon, [took questions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftjG7pbLdpc&t=2s) from the crowd, saying that the drones were safe, popular and unobtrusive. He said the operation would start with about six of them (a decrease from the 10 to 12 he had discussed with the town in mid-August).

“We do hear a lot of feedback from our customers that we’re not fast enough, so that is the exact problem we’re trying to solve,” said Mr. Wafaie, who did not return an emailed request for comment. “Our customers are demanding this service.”

A lot of those, he added, are “single mothers who need diapers because they’re home with a sick child, and they can’t go out.”

The crowd groaned.

Image

Dan Kline is among the founders of a grass-roots group fighting the drone deliveries in Westborough.

When Mr. Wafaie compared the drone noise to the sound made by someone holding an electric toothbrush, a high-pitched buzz filled the room. Someone had brought an electric toothbrush, and held it up. “That’s annoying!” said one woman.

“All day long, horrible!” another said.

For a second, Ms. Farmer laughed. Having watched many video posts of Amazon drones flying, she felt that the toothbrush came nowhere close to how loud they were.

Ms. Farmer has been sensitive to noise since sustaining a head injury in a car crash nearly a decade ago. When her neighbors mow their lawns or clear leaves with a blower, she has to run to the other side of her house. But at least those sounds fade quickly, she told herself. The drones would be relentless.

No one in the crowd spoke in favor of the drones. Instead, residents badgered Mr. Wafaie about safety, privacy and home values. Would Amazon would fly more drones and bigger ones? Could residents stop this program if they didn’t like it?

Several times, he said that they would not like his answer.

Amazon backing out of a drone hub wherever people don’t want it, he said, “would probably not happen.”

“We have a program that we are scaling,” he added.

Dan Kline, a Westborough resident, said in an interview that he assumed the company would have that stance. Scaling business, he said, is “what Amazon does.”

“There’s an air of arrogance that, ‘We’re Amazon and we’re going to this no matter what anyone says, or no matter what anyone wants,” he said. “But this is our town, not Amazon’s.”

Image

In October, more than 500 people packed the high school auditorium to vote on a proposed bylaw that would limit drones.

items.title: Anthropic Is Set to Finalize Pricing for Blockbuster I.P.O.
items.summary: The A.I. company is expected to officially price its shares on Wednesday, and its stock will begin trading on Thursday.
items.full_text:
Title: Anthropic Is Set to Finalize Pricing for Blockbuster I.P.O. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/anthropic-ipo-pricing.html

Published Time: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 18:34:12 GMT

Markdown Content:
[Anthropic](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/technology/anthropic-ipo-finances.html) on Wednesday is expected to finalize the pricing for its initial public offering, potentially defying a volatile and anxious stock market with robust investor demand for artificial intelligence companies and setting a milestone for the A.I. industry.

The San Francisco-based A.I. company, which makes the Claude chatbot, had set a preliminary price range of $70 to $78 a share. But it has seen strong investor interest, and is likely to set a final price on the high end of that range, if not higher, two people familiar with the company’s offering said.

At $70 to $78 a share, Anthropic would be worth $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion, when all shares are counted. That would mean the company’s offering would be second in size only to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which in June raised $85.7 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation in its public listing.

Anthropic’s shares will begin trading on Thursday on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

The listing comes amid a moment of growing market nervousness. Investors have been fearing that the A.I. boom, which has been fueled by debt, may suddenly deflate. With the midterm elections changing the makeup of Congress, the potential for regulations to slow down A.I. development, including data centers, has increased.

The pricing is expected to be finalized on Wednesday evening. Here’s what to know while you wait.

*   Anthropic’s offering is the first time that public market investors will have the chance to invest in one of the A.I. industry’s “frontier labs,” which are developing the core models underlying the boom. The company’s offering prospectus showed a fast-growing business alongside a narrative of future growth and abundance, including curing diseases and expanding economic prosperity. Revenue soared to $33 billion in the first nine months of the year from $41 million in 2023.

*   The company has had an astonishing rise in just five years. Founded in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic and its Claude chatbot were a somewhat obscure second place player to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But Anthropic’s focus on business tools, including Claude Code, which automates software development, became increasingly popular over the last year.

*   Anthropic is going public partly because building A.I. requires so much money to [pay for computer chips, data processing power and electricity](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/technology/anthropic-ai-computing-power.html). The company has issued convertible debt to fund some of the infrastructure needed to support its business, like chips, computing power and data centers. This debt, which turns into equity in the future, is counted as a loss on Anthropic’s books, resulting in a net loss of $104 billion in the first nine months of the year.

*   The public offering is set to the backdrop of turmoil at A.I, chipmaker Nvidia, after the [ouster last week of the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/12/technology/nvidia-jensen-huang.html). On Tuesday, Nvidia reported that its sales topped $100 billion for the first time in the third quarter, twice as much as a year earlier, showing that its business is robust. The company indicated Mr. Huang was not welcome back — even as the former chief executive [issued a statement](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-statement.html) saying he would welcome a return. Read more about [Mr. Huang’s downfall here](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html).

*   Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever. Read more about [the knives out for Anthropic here](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-openai.html).
